hook.line: Everyone in the café has a version of what would have happened if Rosa had posted those letters. To join the conversation you need one small phrase: "I would have...".
hook.en: I would have sent the letter.

examples.es: Con más tiempo, habría terminado el libro.
examples.en: With more time, I would have finished the book.

examples.es: Vale habría preferido quedarse en Medellín.
examples.en: Vale would have preferred to stay in Medellín.

examples.es: Nosotros no habríamos vendido el café.
examples.en: We wouldn't have sold the café.
Would you (informal) have accepted the job in Toronto?
You all would have arrived late.

rule:
English says "would have" with two small words. Spanish needs two pieces too: *habría* plus the *-ado* or *-ido* form of the verb (*dicho*, *vendido*, *aceptado*).

*yo habría*
*tú habrías*
*él, ella, usted habría*
*nosotros habríamos*
*ustedes, ellos habrían*

Only *habría* changes with the person. The second piece never changes, so it stays *dicho*, whoever speaks. You know *habría* from the ending *-ía* for "would": it is the same idea, one step further back. Put *no* and any *lo* or *la* before *habría*: *No lo habría dicho*.

A few forms are irregular: *hecho* (done), *dicho* (said), *escrito* (written), *visto* (seen), *puesto* (put).
smallPrint: Teachers call this the conditional perfect (*condicional compuesto*): *haber* in the conditional plus the past participle.

options: Do you accept the job in Toronto?
Would you have accepted the job in Toronto?
Did you accept the job in Toronto?

readAndPick.es: Nosotros no habríamos vendido el café.
options: We wouldn't have sold the café.
You all would have arrived late.

readAndPick.es: Vale habría preferido quedarse en Medellín.
options: Vale prefers to stay in Medellín.
Vale had preferred to stay in Medellín.
Vale would have preferred to stay in Medellín.
You would have done the same.

readAndPick.es: Habría ido contigo, pero tenía que trabajar.
options: I will go with you, but I have to work.
I would have gone with you, but I had to work.
I went with you, but I had to work.

yourTurn.prompt: Say "I would have said no." Choose *habría* or *había*, then type the whole sentence: *Yo ___ dicho que no.*
Say "With more time, I would have finished the book." Choose *habría* or *habré*, then type it: *Con más tiempo, ___ terminado el libro.*
yourTurn.answer: Con más tiempo, habría terminado el libro.
accept: Con más tiempo, yo habría terminado el libro.
yourTurn.why: *Habría* carries the "would have"; *terminado* stays the same.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: "We would have eaten here."
Type in Spanish, to a friend: "Would you have accepted the job?"
Type in Spanish: "I would have done the same." (the participle of *hacer* is irregular)
Make it negative: *Yo habría vendido el café.*
yourTurn.answer: Yo no habría vendido el café.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about "we": *Yo habría llamado antes.*
yourTurn.why: Only *habría* changes with the person: *habríamos*; *llamado* stays.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask the same to someone you address as *usted*: *¿Habrías dicho que sí?*
yourTurn.why: With *usted* the verb is like *él*: *habría*, no *-s*.

pitfalls.why: Almost. After *habría* you need the participle (*dicho*), not the infinitive (*decir*).
Close. A few verbs have their own participle: *hecho*, *dicho*, *escrito*, *visto*.
Pronouns like *lo* go before *habría*; they never slip in between.
Almost. *Había* means "had"; for "would have" you need *habría*.

personal: Think of one decision you made this year. Say what you would have done in a different version: *Yo habría...* followed by a participle.
